statement: You reach the ten 5-point questions with 18 minutes left. What is the best plan?

choices.text: Start at the first and work through in order until time runs out
choices.misconception: I worked in order, so a hard early question could eat the time meant for easier later ones.

choices.text: Read all ten quickly, pick the two or three that look most doable, and fill in every answer before the end
Spend the whole time on the last question, since it is the hardest
choices.misconception: I assumed the hardest question is worth the most, but every question in this block scores the same.

choices.text: Answer the ones with the shortest statements
choices.misconception: I used length as a proxy for difficulty, which is not reliable in this block.

choices.text: Divide the time evenly, about 1.8 minutes each
choices.misconception: I spread the time equally, which is too little for the questions I could do and wasted on the ones I could not.

hints: Every question in this block scores the same.
Ten questions at the same value means the aim is to maximise how many you finish, not to conquer the hardest. Spend the first ninety seconds finding out which ones are yours.
Read all ten first, pick the two or three you can genuinely do, work those properly, and fill in a guess on the rest before the end.

solutions.reliable: Every question in this block is worth 5 points, so a hard one is worth no more than an easy one. The plan that maximises marks is therefore: spend the first ninety seconds reading all ten and marking the ones that look tractable; work those properly, because a half-finished 5-point question scores the same as an untouched one; and before the end, fill in an answer for every remaining question, since blanks score nothing and wrong answers cost nothing. The transferable idea: with equal-value questions, the aim is how many you finish, not how hard the ones you attempt are.

whyOnTest: The 5-point block is where the paper is won or lost, and working strictly in order is the plan that leaves the most marks on the table.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
